Nagpur: Lemon Prices Soar to ₹160 per Kg as Heatwave, Erratic Rains Hit Crop

Lemons, which normally become cheaper with the onset of the monsoon, have turned unusually expensive in Nagpur this year, offering a sharp reminder of how extreme weather is disrupting even everyday agricultural produce. From the usual ₹50 to ₹70 a kg for good-quality lemons during the rainy season, retail prices have climbed to around 160 a kg this week and the fruit reaching the market is neither as large nor as good in quality as in the previous two monsoons. Retail prices of the tangy fruit are still higher. Yet, unlike with onions, consumers have raised little hue and cry over the steep rise.
Vegetable vendors attribute the unusual price rise primarily to a steep fall in arrivals from major lemon-growing states, including Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Telangana and Gujarat. "Prolonged heatwaves and inadequate rainfall have severely affected orchards, reducing the availability of marketable fruit," they say. "The supplies that used to range between 10 and 20 tonnes have now been restricted to just about 5 to 7 quintals now," said Devman Raut, a leading vegetable wholesaler and broker at Cotton Market.
Climate Shock Comes Home, Lemon Soars to ₹160 per kg
According to him, traders usually rely on cold storage to regulate supplies when arrivals are high. However, with the crop itself affected across major producing states, there is little surplus available to bridge the gap. The shortage has forced Nagpur's markets to increasingly depend on supplies from nearby areas such as Katol, Mohpa, Mowad, Narkhed, Shendurjanaghat, Pandhurna and adjoining tehsils. Farmers point to the weather pattern of the past two years as an important factor behind the crop stress.
Progressive farmer Shrikant Deshpande said the problem began with the failure of crucial rains during the late-winter period. "In 2025, we did not receive the rains that normally come around Holi and Mahashivratri. The same pattern was repeated in 2026, while temperatures touched 48 degrees Celsius for several days," Deshpande said.
"The summer also stretched well into June, placing additional stress on fruit-bearing trees. No rain around Holi and Mahashivratri meant groundwater table fell, while moisture in the soil and air also remained extremely low. As a result, fruit trees could not withstand the prolonged heatwave, said Shrikant Deshpande, farmer. The lemon crisis illustrates a broader agricultural concern - when extreme heat combines with erratic rainfall, its impact is felt not only in farms but eventually in urban markets and household budgets, said Raut.
